issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising second-appellate jurisdiction cannot set aside concurrent findings of fact by reappraising the evidence without a substantial question of law.
material_facts: The trial court found that the tenant had sublet parts of the premises and caused a nuisance by obstructing the landlord’s passage; the first appellate court upheld those findings.
The subletting finding rested on testimony from persons said to have occupied the sublet premises, and the obstruction finding was supported by a commissioner’s report.
The High Court reversed the concurrent findings, relying on a lack of detail in the pleadings and its assessment of the evidence, without formulating a substantial question of law.
The Supreme Court found no case of no evidence or perverse findings; it observed that details omitted from pleadings could be supplied through evidence.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s reversal of the concurrent findings was unsustainable. The findings of subletting and nuisance, and the eviction decree based on them, were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 CPC, as amended in 1976, confines a second appeal to a case involving a substantial question of law. The High Court must formulate that question and hear the appeal on it; the existence of such a question is a condition for exercising jurisdiction. Concurrent findings based on evidence cannot be displaced merely by reappraising that evidence, and lack of detail in pleadings alone is not a reason to set them aside where evidence supplies the details. The Court relied on Panchugopal Barua v. Umesh Chandra Goswami, Kshitish Chandra Purkait v. Santosh Kumar Purkait, Ram Prasad Rajak v. Nand Kumar & Bros, and Kondiba Dagadu Kadam v. Savitribai Sopan Gujar. The eviction findings concerned subletting and nuisance under Sections 13(1)(e) and 13(1)(d) of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950.

rule.if: second_appeal and concurrent_factual_findings and findings_supported_by_evidence and high_court_reversed_by_reappraising_evidence and substantial_question_not_formulated and no_evidence_or_perversity_not_shown

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding is a second appeal from an appellate decree.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and the first appellate court reached the same findings on factual grounds.
predicates.findings_supported_by_evidence: Evidence in the record supported the concurrent factual findings.
predicates.high_court_reversed_by_reappraising_evid: The High Court set aside the findings after reassessing the evidence.
predicates.substantial_question_not_formulated: The High Court did not formulate a substantial question of law for the appeal.
predicates.no_evidence_or_perversity_not_shown: The record did not show that the findings rested on no evidence or were perverse.

issues.definition: When a second appeal involves concurrent factual findings supported by evidence, the High Court reverses them by reassessing that evidence, no substantial question of law is formulated, and no lack of evidence or perversity is shown, the concurrent findings must stand.

issues.legal_issue: A finding of no rent default left undisturbed by the High Court does not warrant further interference where no substantial question of law arises from that finding.
material_facts: The trial court found rent default, but the first appellate court set aside that finding and found no default.
The High Court did not disturb the first appellate court’s no-default finding.

The parties disputed whether failure to pay rent provisionally fixed in a separate proceeding constituted a default, but the Supreme Court declined to interpret the relevant rent provisions because the findings on subletting and nuisance independently supported eviction.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no error in the High Court’s leaving the no-default finding undisturbed and did not decide the parties’ dispute about the effect of the provisional rent determination.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 CPC limits second appeals to cases involving a substantial question of law. The Court treated the first appellate court’s finding of no default as final because the High Court had not disturbed it, and found no substantial question warranting further interference. It expressly declined to decide the competing interpretations of Sections 7 and 13 of the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950.

predicates.rent_default_issue_in_eviction_proceedin: The proceeding is an eviction case in which rent default is raised as a ground.
predicates.first_appellate_court_found_no_default: The first appellate court found that the tenant had not defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.high_court_left_no_default_finding_undis: The High Court left the first appellate court’s no-default finding unchanged.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding includes a rent-default issue, the first appellate court finds no default, and the High Court leaves that finding unchanged, there is no further interference with the no-default finding.
